procedural_history.impugned_order: Award dated April 7, 1967 of the Industrial Tribunal, Chandigarh in Reference No. 4C of 1966, setting aside the order of the appellant (State Bank of India) discharging the services of the first respondent and directing his reinstatement with full back wages.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: State Bank of India appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the award of the Industrial Tribunal.

directions: The award of the Industrial Tribunal dated April 7, 1967, is confirmed and this appeal is dismissed with costs of the first respondent.

issue.issue_text: Whether the inquiry before an Industrial Tribunal must be conducted in two parts: first, an investigation into the validity of the domestic inquiry, and if it is found invalid, then a further inquiry where the management can adduce evidence to justify its action.

facts: The Supreme Court noted a difference of opinion among various High Courts on this issue.

The Madhya Pradesh and Delhi High Courts held that the inquiry before an Industrial Tribunal should be conducted in two parts: first, a decision on the validity of the management's domestic inquiry, and if found invalid, a second stage for the management to adduce evidence on the merits of its action.
The Orissa High Court held a contrary view, stating the Tribunal was not obligated to give the management a second opportunity to present evidence after finding the domestic inquiry defective.
law: The issue referred to an Industrial Tribunal is the broad question of whether the management was justified in its action (e.g., dismissal), not the narrow question of whether the domestic inquiry was conducted properly.
The management has the right to defend its action by arguing that its domestic inquiry was valid.
The management also has the right to adduce independent evidence before the Tribunal to justify its action on the facts, regardless of the validity of the domestic inquiry.
It is the management's decision and responsibility to choose its line of defense and present all its evidence accordingly.
application: The Supreme Court described the proceeding before the Tribunal as a "composite inquiry," not a two-part process.
The Court reasoned that since the management has the right to present evidence on the merits from the beginning, there is no need to split the inquiry into two stages.
If the management chooses to defend its action *solely* on the basis that its domestic inquiry was valid, and the Tribunal finds the inquiry to be invalid, the management will lose the case.

Alternatively, the management can choose to both defend the inquiry's validity and simultaneously present evidence on the merits. In this scenario, the Tribunal can still rule in the management's favor based on the evidence, even if it finds the domestic inquiry was flawed.
The Court concluded that forcing a two-part inquiry is unjustified and that it is up to the management to present its full case during the single, composite proceeding.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the inquiry must be conducted in two parts. It held that the proceeding before the Tribunal is a single, composite inquiry where the management must decide its strategy and present all its evidence, including any justification on the merits, without being entitled to a second opportunity after a ruling on the domestic inquiry's validity.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is open to the management to justify its order of dismissal or discharge by adducing independent evidence before the Tribunal, even if the domestic inquiry is found to be defective or if no inquiry was held at all.

facts: The issue before the court is whether management can present new, independent evidence before an Industrial Tribunal to justify a dismissal, especially when its internal domestic inquiry is found to be defective or was never conducted.
law: The Supreme Court affirmed that management has a right to sustain its order of dismissal or discharge by adducing independent evidence before the Tribunal.
This right applies even if the domestic inquiry is found to be defective or if no inquiry was held at all. The Court stated that a defective inquiry stands on the same footing as no inquiry.
In such cases, the entire matter is open before the Tribunal, and the employer must justify on the facts that its order of dismissal was proper.

The inquiry conducted by the Tribunal is a single, composite inquiry. The Court rejected the view that the inquiry must be conducted in two parts (first ruling on the domestic inquiry's validity, then taking new evidence).
application: It is the management's choice to decide its strategy before the Tribunal. It can choose to defend its action solely on the basis of its domestic inquiry, or it can also present new evidence to justify the dismissal on its merits.
If the management relies only on the domestic inquiry and the Tribunal finds it invalid, the management's case will fail.
However, if the management adduces new evidence, the Tribunal can accept that evidence and rule in the management's favor, even if it finds the original domestic inquiry was invalid.

The responsibility lies with the management to avail itself of this right to present evidence. It is not an obligation for the Tribunal to first invalidate the domestic inquiry and then offer the management a separate opportunity to present new evidence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court decided that it is open to the management to justify its order of dismissal or discharge by adducing independent evidence before the Tribunal. This right exists even if the domestic inquiry is found to be defective or if no inquiry was held at all, as the Tribunal can then decide the case on its merits based on the evidence presented before it.

issue.issue_text: Whether the management fails in its case if it chooses to defend its action solely on the validity of its domestic inquiry, and the Tribunal finds that inquiry to be improper, without the management having adduced any independent evidence to justify its action on the facts.

facts: The management defended its decision to discharge an employee before the Industrial Tribunal.
The management's strategy was to justify its action *solely* on the basis that the domestic inquiry it had conducted was proper and valid.
The management did not offer to produce any independent evidence before the Tribunal to prove the facts of the employee's misconduct.
law: When defending a dismissal or discharge before a Tribunal, the management has two options: a) defend its action solely on the basis that its domestic inquiry was proper, or b) rely on the domestic inquiry and also adduce independent evidence to justify its action on the facts.
The choice of which strategy to adopt is entirely a matter for the management.

The inquiry conducted by the Tribunal is a single, composite inquiry. It is not a two-part process where the Tribunal first rules on the validity of the domestic inquiry and then gives the management a second chance to present evidence on the merits if the inquiry is found to be defective.
application: The Court applied the legal principle to the facts by stating that if the management chooses the first option—to rely solely on its domestic inquiry—it takes a risk.
If the Tribunal then finds that the domestic inquiry was improper or invalid, the management's entire defense fails because it has presented no other evidence to justify its action.
Conversely, if the management had chosen to adduce independent evidence, it could still have won its case on the merits, even if the Tribunal found the domestic inquiry to be invalid.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that if the management chooses to defend its action solely on the validity of its domestic inquiry, and the Tribunal finds that inquiry to be improper, the management will fail in its case. The management cannot later complain about not having an opportunity to present evidence on the facts, as it was its own strategic decision not to do so during the Tribunal's composite inquiry.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the management fails in its case if it chooses to defend its action solely on the validity of its domestic inquiry, and the Tribunal finds that inquiry to be improper, without the management having adduced any independent evidence to justify its action on the facts.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's case should not fail simply because the domestic inquiry was found to be improper and no other evidence was adduced. (This argument is inferred from the court's rejection of the Solicitor-General's 'third contention').

cases.case_name: M / s. Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. Their Workers
cases.principle: The case was approved by the court in the context of establishing the correct procedure to be followed.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In awarding punishment by way of disciplinary action, an order should be passed after due consideration of all the relevant facts and circumstances.
obiter: It has been held by this Court in Workmen of Motipur Sugar Factory (Private) Ltd. v. Motipur Sugar Factory.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While management has the right to adduce independent evidence before an Industrial Tribunal to justify a dismissal, even if its domestic inquiry is found to be defective, this right must be exercised. If the management chooses to defend its action solely on the basis of the domestic inquiry and does not request an opportunity to present further evidence, its case will fail if the Tribunal finds the inquiry to be improper. The onus is on the management to avail itself of the opportunity to justify its action on the merits before the Tribunal.
legal_tests_applied: Principles of Natural Justice: The court assesses whether the domestic inquiry provided the workman a reasonable opportunity to defend himself, including the right to cross-examine witnesses and adduce evidence in support of his defence.
Tribunal's Power of Interference: A Tribunal is justified in interfering with a management's order of discharge when the principles of natural justice have been violated in the domestic inquiry.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant (management) chose to justify its order of discharge solely on the basis of its domestic inquiry, which the Tribunal found to be in violation of the principles of natural justice.
Despite having a right to adduce independent evidence before the Tribunal to justify its action, the appellant never asked for such an opportunity nor availed of it.

The appellant did not make a grievance in its Special Leave Petition that the Tribunal had failed to provide an opportunity to adduce evidence, which confirms that it had consciously chosen not to do so.
why_respondent_won: The Tribunal correctly found that the domestic inquiry was vitiated because it violated the principles of natural justice by not summoning witnesses requested by the workman.

The appellant's case before the Tribunal rested entirely on the validity of the flawed domestic inquiry, and since that foundation was invalid and no other evidence was offered, the management's justification for the discharge failed.
policy_considerations: The court balances the management's right to justify its disciplinary actions with the procedural obligation to present its full case before the Tribunal. A party cannot rely exclusively on a potentially flawed internal process and then, after it is invalidated, claim it was denied a chance to present evidence it never offered.

The proceeding before the Tribunal is the ultimate forum for adjudication. Both the workman and the management have a right to present their case fully. The management has a right to defend its action on the merits, but it must actively seek to exercise this right if its initial domestic inquiry is challenged.
